opus-5.5.text:
Agentic workloads stress attention in ways that standard chat or single-turn question answering doesn't. When a model acts as an agent, it isn't answering one question. It's running a long loop: calling tools, reading the results, revising its plan, and sometimes working over hours or across thousands of steps. So the context isn't a tidy prompt anymore. It's a growing trajectory of observations, actions, errors, and intermediate reasoning.

The first issue is length. Full attention scales quadratically with sequence length, and the KV cache grows linearly, so serving very long trajectories gets expensive in both compute and memory. We've made a lot of progress on long context, with techniques like sparse and local attention, grouped-query and multi-query attention to shrink the cache, and better positional schemes. But having a long context window is different from using it well. You can fit a million tokens and still have the model lose track of something critical from step twelve when it's on step four hundred.

That points to the second issue, which I think matters more: selectivity. In an agentic setting, most of the context is noise at any given moment. Tool outputs are verbose, logs are long, and many earlier steps no longer matter. What you want is a mechanism that can decide what to retain, compress, and retrieve, closer to how a person keeps a working memory and refers back to notes when needed. So I expect attention to move toward hybrid designs. You'd have dense attention over a recent working window, plus some form of compressed or retrieved memory for the longer history. That memory could be learned summarization, state-space-style recurrent components, or explicit retrieval over the agent's own past.

The third issue is credit assignment over long horizons. If an agent makes a decision early that only proves wrong much later, the model has to connect those events. That's partly a training problem, around reinforcement learning on multi-step tasks, but it interacts with architecture. The model needs a reliable path to attend back to the decisions that matter, and training has to teach it to do that rather than just attend to whatever is recent.

Finally, there's an efficiency angle that people underestimate. Agents spend a lot of time re-reading the same context: the same system instructions, the same tool definitions, the same documents. So prefix caching, reusing KV states across calls, and handling branching trajectories, where an agent explores several options from a shared state, all become important. Some of that is systems work rather than modeling, but at this point the two are tightly coupled.

So in short, I don't think the answer is just "make the window bigger." It's making attention more structured: efficient over the recent past, selective about the distant past, and trained to keep the right things in focus over a long sequence of actions.

r001.rationale: It proposes compressed or retrieved memory for the longer history alongside a recent working window, communicating access to information beyond that window.

r002.rationale: It mentions learned summarization generally, but does not identify summarized collected articles as a requirement for a research agent.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that attention as we have it today was designed for a fundamentally different regime than the one agents live in. The original transformer was built around a bounded sequence: you have a document, you have a prompt, you attend over all of it, and you produce an output. Agents break almost every one of those assumptions. The context isn't bounded, it's a stream. The relevant information isn't uniformly distributed, it's extremely sparse and spiky. And the model is no longer just reading, it's acting, observing the consequences, and reading again, so the context is partly something it created itself.

So the first thing I'd say is that the quadratic cost problem, which people have been working on for years, becomes qualitatively different in the agentic setting. When you're running a long-horizon task with tool calls, you might have hundreds of thousands of tokens of trajectory, and most of it is scaffolding: tool outputs, intermediate reasoning, failed attempts. The question isn't just "can we attend over a million tokens cheaply," it's "should we be attending over most of this at all." I think we'll see a lot more structure where the model is doing something closer to retrieval over its own history, with hierarchical or compressed representations of past steps, rather than flat dense attention over every token it has ever seen. Some of that will be learned compression of the KV cache, some of it will be explicit memory modules, and I suspect the right answer is a mix.

The second piece is that attention needs to become much more selective about what it trusts. In an agentic loop, a big chunk of your context is coming from the environment: web pages, file contents, outputs from other tools or other models. That's very different from a carefully curated prompt. So you want the model to attend differently to instructions versus observations, to have something like a notion of provenance. Right now that's mostly handled by formatting and training, but I think architecturally there's room for attention to carry more information about where a token came from and how much weight it should get.

Third, and this is the one I find most interesting, is the temporal dimension. Agents revisit the same state many times. They plan, they act, they come back. Standard attention is memoryless across forward passes; everything has to be reconstructed from the context window each time. I think we'll see architectures that maintain persistent state across steps, so the model isn't re-deriving its understanding of the task from scratch on every call. That's partially a systems question about caching, but it's also a modeling question about what you carry forward and how you update it when the world changes underneath you.

And then finally there's a very practical point: latency. Agents make many sequential calls, so per-step inference cost compounds in a way that doesn't matter for a single chat response. Techniques like sparse attention, multi-query and grouped-query attention, speculative approaches, all of that becomes much more important when you're doing fifty steps instead of one.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say attention needs to go from being a mechanism that reads a sequence to being a mechanism that manages a working memory: deciding what to keep, what to compress, what to trust, and what to carry into the next step. I don't think we have the final form of that yet, but the pressure from agentic workloads is going to push the architecture there faster than pure language modeling ever did.

r001.rationale: The response says agent contexts are unbounded and proposes retrieval over history, compressed past steps, and persistent state, communicating the need to use information beyond the current context window.

r002.rationale: It mentions compressed representations of past steps and tool outputs, but does not identify a summarized representation of collected articles for a research agent.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what does an agent need to pay attention to as it interacts with an environment over time? It has the current request, but it also has previous observations, actions it has taken, and results from tools. Some of that information becomes relevant much later. So the challenge is not just supporting a longer context; it is identifying and retaining the information that matters for the next decision.

Attention is one part of that. You can imagine combining attention over the immediate context with a memory mechanism that retrieves relevant information from earlier interactions. And that has to be efficient, because an agent may go through many steps before completing a task. Processing the entire history at every step can become very expensive.

I would also separate the architectural question from the learning question. Giving a model access to more information does not necessarily teach it when to look back, when to seek a new observation, or when it has enough evidence to act. We need training and evaluation that exercise those behaviors over multiple steps. The evolution is really in how attention, memory, and learning work together to support reliable decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent needs to retain information from earlier interactions and retrieve it alongside the immediate context, conveying access to information beyond the current context window.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify a summarized representation of collected articles as something the attention mechanism needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think attention needs to evolve from helping a model understand a single context to helping it decide what information matters over a sequence of actions. For an agent, that includes the original goal, what it has already tried, feedback from tools, and what has changed in its environment.

A longer context window helps, but it doesn’t solve that whole problem. The agent needs to retrieve relevant information, maintain useful state, and avoid spending the same amount of computation on every observation. So I think selective attention and memory need to work much more closely together.

And attention is only one piece. You also need training that teaches the model when to act, when to gather more information, and when to revise its plan. The important question is whether those mechanisms help the agent make reliable progress over longer tasks.

r001.rationale: The response mentions longer context windows, retrieval, and maintaining state, but does not clearly identify referring to information beyond the current context window as a requirement.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a research agent or a summarized representation of collected articles.
